slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page comparison, in your own words, of the "it works on my machine" problem Northbridge Retail's team hits and why a VM-per-app fix is heavier than it needs to be, then check Task Manager/Activity Monitor or `docker info` on your own machine to see how many CPU cores and how much memory are available before you install anything.
slots.deliverable: A written note contrasting containers vs. VMs for Northbridge's catalog/checkout split, plus your machine's `docker info`-reported CPU and memory baseline.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a container with `docker run -d --name probe ubuntu sleep 300`, then from inside it run `ps aux` and `hostname` to see its isolated process list and hostname, and from the host run `ps aux | grep sleep` to see that same process visible to the host OS -- concretely showing a shared kernel with isolated namespaces.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing the same sleep process as PID 1 inside the container's namespace and as a normal PID on the host.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine on Linux) on your own machine, then confirm it's working with `docker version` (showing both Client and Server sections) and `docker run hello-world`.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output from `docker version` and a successful `docker run hello-world` on your own machine.

slots.practicalActivity: Run `docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx`, confirm the default nginx page loads at http://localhost:8080 in a real browser, then run `docker ps` to see the running container and `docker stop` it by its container ID.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the nginx welcome page at localhost:8080, plus terminal output of `docker ps` showing the running container before you stopped it.

slots.practicalActivity: Pull three real images with different tags -- `docker pull node:20`, `docker pull node:20-alpine`, `docker pull redis:7` -- then run `docker images` and compare the Alpine-based node image's size against the full one, confirming for yourself why Alpine variants exist.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of `docker images` showing all three pulled images with their actual sizes, plus a one-sentence note on the size difference between node:20 and node:20-alpine.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a container with `docker run -d --name lifecycle-test redis:7`, then walk it through every state with `docker stop lifecycle-test`, `docker start lifecycle-test`, `docker pause lifecycle-test`, `docker unpause lifecycle-test`, and finally `docker rm -f lifecycle-test`, checking `docker ps -a` after each command to see the status column change.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of `docker ps -a` captured after each lifecycle command, showing the container's status transition from created through removed.

slots.practicalActivity: Run `docker run -d -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devops123 --name pg-test postgres:16`, confirm the port mapping with `docker port pg-test`, then tail its startup output with `docker logs -f pg-test` until you see "database system is ready to accept connections."
slots.deliverable: Terminal output from `docker port pg-test` showing the real port mapping, plus the log line confirming Postgres finished starting.

slots.practicalActivity: With `pg-test` still running from the previous slot, open a real interactive shell into it with `docker exec -it pg-test bash`, run `psql -U postgres -c "SELECT version();"` from inside the container, then exit and use `docker inspect pg-test` to find its internal IP address and mounted volumes from the host side.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of the Postgres version returned from inside the container via `docker exec`, plus the relevant `docker inspect` fields (IP address, mounts) read from the host.

slots.practicalActivity: Before cleanup, run `docker system df` to see current disk usage by images, containers, and volumes, then stop and remove every container from this chapter's labs with `docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq)`, remove unused images with `docker image prune -a`, and run `docker system df` again to confirm the space was reclaimed.
slots.deliverable: Two `docker system df` outputs -- before and after cleanup -- showing real disk space reclaimed.

slots.practicalActivity: Dedicated lab: start three unrelated containers (`nginx`, `redis:7`, `postgres:16` with an env password), deliberately misconfigure one port mapping, then use only `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `docker inspect`, and `docker exec` -- no restarting anything -- to diagnose which container is misconfigured and why, writing down your diagnostic steps as you go.
slots.deliverable: A written diagnostic log showing the sequence of `docker ps`/`logs`/`inspect`/`exec` commands you ran and the misconfiguration you found, without having restarted the broken container to "fix" it blindly.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real Dockerfile for a tiny Node.js or Python "hello world" app using FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, and CMD, then build it with `docker build -t northbridge/hello:1.0 .` and run it with `docker run northbridge/hello:1.0` to confirm it actually works.
slots.deliverable: A real Dockerfile plus terminal output showing a successful `docker build` and `docker run` of your own image.

slots.practicalActivity: Reorder your Dockerfile from the previous slot so `COPY package.json`/`requirements.txt` and the install step come before `COPY . .`, rebuild twice (changing only an app file, not a dependency, between builds), and compare the build times and `CACHED` lines in the output to see layer caching working.
slots.deliverable: Two build outputs showing the dependency-install layer served from cache on the second build while the app-code layer rebuilt.

slots.practicalActivity: Build two versions of a small image -- one using only CMD, one using ENTRYPOINT with a default CMD argument -- then run each with `docker run <image>` and `docker run <image> --some-flag` to see concretely how ENTRYPOINT's fixed command differs from CMD's fully overridable one.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output from running both image variants with and without an override argument, showing the behavioral difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT.

slots.practicalActivity: Take a small frontend or compiled app, write a single-stage Dockerfile for it and record the image size with `docker images`, then rewrite it as a real multi-stage build (FROM ... AS build, then COPY --from=build into a minimal nginx or alpine runtime stage) and compare the two sizes directly, the way Northbridge's catalog frontend went from 900MB+ to under 50MB.
slots.deliverable: Two `docker images` size readings -- single-stage vs. multi-stage -- for the same app, plus the multi-stage Dockerfile itself.

slots.practicalActivity: Take your multi-stage image from the previous slot and apply at least two further size cuts (swap the runtime base for an -alpine or -slim variant, add a .dockerignore excluding node_modules/.git, combine RUN commands to cut layers), rebuilding and recording the size after each change.
slots.deliverable: A table of image sizes after each optimization step applied to your own multi-stage image, with the .dockerignore file used.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a free Docker Hub account (if you don't have one), run `docker login`, tag your hello-world image from Chapter 3 as `<your-dockerhub-username>/hello:1.0`, push it with `docker push`, then pull it back down under a different local tag to confirm a round trip through a real public registry.
slots.deliverable: A real image pushed to your own Docker Hub account, with terminal output of both the push and a successful re-pull under a new tag.

slots.practicalActivity: Tag the same image three ways -- a semantic version (1.0.0), a build-specific tag, and :latest -- push all three to Docker Hub, then open the AWS Console's ECR service and manually create one private repository (no push required unless you have CLI access configured) to see the registry hostname and push commands ECR itself generates for an image.
slots.deliverable: Three real tags of the same image visible in your Docker Hub repository's tag list, plus a screenshot of an ECR repository you created showing its generated push commands.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a Postgres container with a named volume (`-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`), create a table and insert a row via `docker exec ... psql`, remove the container with `docker rm -f`, then start a brand-new container reusing the same named volume and confirm the row is still there -- then separately run a container with a bind mount (`-v $(pwd)/html:/usr/share/nginx/html`) and edit a file on the host to see it change live inside the container.
slots.deliverable: Proof that data survived container removal via the named volume (the recovered row), plus a screenshot of a live edit through a bind mount reflecting instantly in the running container.

slots.practicalActivity: Run `docker network ls` to see Docker's default bridge, host, and none networks, then start two containers on the default bridge and try to reach one from the other by container name (it fails) and then by IP via `docker inspect` (it works) -- directly demonstrating why the default bridge doesn't give you name-based discovery.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing a failed ping/curl by container name on the default bridge, followed by a successful one by IP address.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real user-defined bridge network with `docker network create catalog-net`, start two containers attached to it with `--network catalog-net`, and confirm one can now reach the other by container name alone (e.g. `docker exec app1 ping app2`) -- the fix for the previous slot's failed name resolution.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing a successful ping or curl between two containers by name on a real user-defined network you created.

slots.practicalActivity: On your user-defined network from the previous slot, start a third container and have it resolve the second container's name with `docker exec app3 getent hosts app2` (or `nslookup app2` if available) to see Docker's embedded DNS resolve a service name to its current container IP without you hardcoding anything.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of a DNS lookup resolving a container name to its IP address via Docker's embedded DNS on your user-defined network.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real compose.yaml for one service (e.g. nginx with a port mapping) and bring it up with `docker compose up -d`, confirm it with `docker compose ps` and a browser request, then tear it down with `docker compose down` and bring it back up again to see the whole cycle work from one file.
slots.deliverable: A real compose.yaml for one service, plus terminal output of `docker compose up`, `docker compose ps`, and `docker compose down`.

slots.practicalActivity: Write Northbridge's three-service compose.yaml for real: a `web` service, an `api` service with `depends_on: - db` and `DB_HOST: db`, and a `db` Postgres service with a named volume, bring the whole stack up with `docker compose up -d`, and confirm in the startup output that Compose started them in dependency order (db, then api, then web).
slots.deliverable: A real three-service compose.yaml plus terminal output of `docker compose up` showing the three containers starting in dependency order.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real `healthcheck:` block to the db service in your three-service compose.yaml (e.g. `pg_isready`) and `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy` on api, plus a `restart: unless-stopped` policy on every service, then bring the stack down and up again and watch `docker compose ps` show api waiting until db reports healthy before starting -- closing the readiness gap `depends_on` alone left open.
slots.deliverable: An updated compose.yaml with health checks and restart policies on every service, plus `docker compose ps` output showing api waiting on db's healthy status.

slots.practicalActivity: Move every hardcoded credential out of your compose.yaml into a real .env file (e.g. POSTGRES_PASSWORD), reference it with `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` in compose.yaml, add .env to a real .gitignore, and confirm `docker compose up -d` still works by reading the value from .env instead of the file itself.
slots.deliverable: A compose.yaml with no hardcoded secrets, a .env file supplying them, and a .gitignore excluding .env, with a successful `docker compose up` confirming the substitution worked.

slots.practicalActivity: Add `deploy: resources: limits: cpus: '0.5' memory: 256M` to one service in your compose.yaml, bring the stack up, and confirm the real enforced limit with `docker stats` while the container is running -- then try to run a small memory-stress command inside it to see the limit actually bite.
slots.deliverable: A compose.yaml service with real CPU and memory limits, plus `docker stats` output confirming those limits are enforced on the running container.

slots.practicalActivity: Run `docker logs --tail 50 -f` against one of your running services while generating some traffic against it, then run `docker stats --no-stream` across your whole stack to capture a point-in-time CPU/memory snapshot of every container at once.
slots.deliverable: Captured `docker logs` output showing real log lines from traffic you generated, plus a `docker stats --no-stream` snapshot of your full stack.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a non-root USER instruction to one of your own Dockerfiles from Chapter 3 (create a dedicated user, chown the app directory to it), rebuild and confirm with `docker exec <container> whoami` that it's no longer root, then read through a real Kubernetes Pod YAML example online and write two sentences on which of your compose.yaml concepts (named volumes, service names, depends_on) map to which Kubernetes concept.
slots.deliverable: A rebuilt image confirmed to run as a non-root user via `docker exec whoami`, plus a short written mapping of compose.yaml concepts to their Kubernetes equivalents.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Containerize a Multi-Service Application

slots.practicalActivity: Read the full capstone rubric and, before writing any code, draft a written plan naming your own three services (your own catalog/checkout/db equivalent, real or a project you already have), which Dockerfile needs a multi-stage build, and which network and volume each service will need.
slots.deliverable: A written capstone plan naming your three services and mapping each rubric item (multi-stage builds, user-defined network, named volume, health checks, resource limits, non-root users, .env secrets, registry push) to how you'll satisfy it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the real capstone: multi-stage Dockerfiles for your two application services, a compose.yaml wiring all three services on a user-defined network with a named volume for the database, health checks and restart policies on every service, resource limits, non-root users in both Dockerfiles, secrets pulled from a gitignored .env, and both application images pushed to your Docker Hub account with real version tags -- then run `docker compose up -d` from a clean checkout and confirm `docker compose ps` shows all three healthy.
slots.deliverable: A working multi-service repo (Dockerfiles, compose.yaml, .env.example, .gitignore) satisfying every rubric item, plus `docker compose ps` output showing all three services healthy and both images visible on Docker Hub.

slots.practicalActivity: Push your capstone repo to a public GitHub repository with a real README documenting how to run it (`docker compose up -d`, required .env vars, how to verify it's healthy), then write the portfolio paragraph you'd actually show an interviewer: what the three services are, which rubric items you implemented, and one specific production-hardening decision you made and why.
slots.deliverable: A public GitHub repo with your capstone code and a real README, plus a written portfolio paragraph ready to show in a job interview.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can write production-ready Dockerfiles with multi-stage builds, push images to a real registry, and ship a hardened multi-service application with Docker Compose -- networked, health-checked, resource-limited, and secrets-free -- the exact containerization foundation the Kubernetes course ahead in this path builds on.
